sql: CREATE PROCEDURE find_order(IN p_id INT, IN p_id INT) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = p_id;

sql: SELECT department_id, employee_name, MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;

sql: SELECT c.id, o.id AS paid_order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'paid';

schema_context: customers(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY); orders(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT, status VARCHAR(20))
seed_data: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1),(2); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,'paid');
expected_behavior: Return customer 1 with order 10 and customer 2 with a NULL paid_order_id.
root_cause: The WHERE predicate rejects the NULL-complemented right side of the LEFT JOIN, effectively retaining only matching paid rows.
reference_fix_sql: SELECT c.id, o.id AS paid_order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid';
reference_explanation: Make paid status part of the join condition so it restricts eligible order matches without filtering away unmatched customers.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL JOIN documentation demonstrates LEFT JOIN conditions in ON and NULL-based handling of unmatched right rows.

semantic_check.expected: Both sample customers remain, and customer 2 has a NULL right-side id.
semantic_check.observed: The ON-clause placement follows the documented LEFT JOIN form.

verification.details: The two-row expected result is specified but not executed.

notes: Runtime test pending; no MariaDB compatibility claim is made.

sql: SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.total) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id GROUP BY o.customer_id;
user_problem: Customer order totals are inflated whenever an order has multiple payment rows, although the SQL appears to use the correct foreign key.
schema_context: orders(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT, total DECIMAL(12,2)); payments(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, order_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(12,2))
seed_data: INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,7,100); INSERT INTO payments VALUES (10,1,60),(11,1,40);
expected_behavior: Return order_total 100 for customer 7 rather than counting the order once per payment.
root_cause: Joining orders to every payment multiplies each order row before SUM(o.total), so the aggregate runs over a one-to-many fanout.
reference_fix_sql: SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.total) AS order_total FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id) GROUP BY o.customer_id;
reference_explanation: Use EXISTS when payment presence is the only requirement, preserving one input row per order before SUM.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL JOIN grammar documents joined table references and ON search conditions that produce the pre-aggregation row set.
The MySQL SUM entry documents aggregation over the expression values in the selected group.

semantic_check.expected: The sample customer total is 100 despite two matching payment rows.
semantic_check.observed: EXISTS removes the one-to-many row multiplication before the documented SUM operation.

verification.details: The relational oracle is explicit, but no MySQL execution was performed.

notes: The repair assumes only orders with at least one payment should be included.

sql: SELECT i.id, r.rate FROM invoices i JOIN exchange_rates r WHERE i.issued_on = CURRENT_DATE;
user_problem: Today's invoices are duplicated once for every exchange-rate row. The developer expected JOIN alone to match currencies automatically.
schema_context: invoices(id BIGINT, currency CHAR(3), issued_on DATE); exchange_rates(currency CHAR(3), rate DECIMAL(12,6))
expected_behavior: Return each invoice with only the rate for its own currency.
root_cause: The JOIN has no ON or USING condition; in MySQL bare JOIN is equivalent to an inner or cross join and therefore pairs unrelated rows.
reference_fix_sql: SELECT i.id, r.rate FROM invoices i JOIN exchange_rates r ON r.currency = i.currency WHERE i.issued_on = CURRENT_DATE;
reference_explanation: Add an ON predicate connecting the two currency columns so only the intended rate row joins to each invoice.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL JOIN documentation states that JOIN, CROSS JOIN, and INNER JOIN are syntactic equivalents and distinguishes use of an ON clause.

semantic_check.expected: Each invoice matches rates having the same currency code.
semantic_check.observed: The repair supplies the ON search condition described by MySQL JOIN syntax.

verification.details: Documentation-only; currency uniqueness should be enforced or tested separately.

sql: UPDATE orders SET region_name = r.name FROM regions r WHERE r.id = orders.region_id;
user_problem: A PostgreSQL UPDATE FROM statement must populate cached region names after migration to MySQL without changing which rows match.
schema_context: orders(id BIGINT, region_id BIGINT, region_name VARCHAR(100)); regions(id BIGINT, name VARCHAR(100))
expected_behavior: Set each order region_name from the regions row whose id equals region_id.
root_cause: MySQL multiple-table UPDATE expresses the joined tables before SET rather than using PostgreSQL's FROM clause.
reference_fix_sql: UPDATE orders AS o JOIN regions AS r ON r.id = o.region_id SET o.region_name = r.name;
reference_explanation: Rewrite the source relation as a MySQL joined table reference before SET and retain the same equality condition in ON.

The MySQL JOIN grammar supplies the table reference and ON condition used in the repair.

sql: SELECT s.id, t.id FROM staging_contacts s JOIN contacts t ON s.external_id = t.external_id;
user_problem: The reconciliation intentionally treats two missing external IDs as the same placeholder, but rows where both keys are NULL never join.
schema_context: staging_contacts(id BIGINT, external_id VARCHAR(80) NULL); contacts(id BIGINT, external_id VARCHAR(80) NULL)
seed_data: INSERT INTO staging_contacts VALUES (1,NULL); INSERT INTO contacts VALUES (9,NULL);
expected_behavior: Match the two sample rows because both external_id values are NULL under the stated business rule.
root_cause: Ordinary equality yields NULL for NULL operands, so the ON predicate does not become true when both join keys are missing.
reference_fix_sql: SELECT s.id, t.id FROM staging_contacts s JOIN contacts t ON s.external_id <=> t.external_id;
reference_explanation: Use MySQL's NULL-safe equality operator in the join condition so two NULL keys compare as equal.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL <=> documentation states that two NULL operands return true while one NULL and one non-NULL return false.

semantic_check.expected: The sample produces the pair (1,9).
semantic_check.observed: The documented <=> truth behavior meets the explicit placeholder rule.

verification.details: The sample was not executed; the business decision to equate missing keys must be human-verified.

sql: SELECT id FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM blocked_users);
user_problem: The allow-list query unexpectedly returns nothing whenever blocked_users contains a row whose user_id is NULL.
schema_context: users(id BIGINT NOT NULL); blocked_users(user_id BIGINT NULL)
seed_data: INSERT INTO users VALUES (1),(2); INSERT INTO blocked_users VALUES (2),(NULL);
expected_behavior: Return user 1 and exclude blocked user 2, regardless of NULL rows in blocked_users.
root_cause: NOT IN negates an IN comparison, and a NULL in the candidate set can leave the predicate unknown for otherwise unmatched ids.
reference_fix_sql: SELECT u.id FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b WHERE b.user_id = u.id);
reference_explanation: Use a correlated NOT EXISTS test so unrelated NULL values in the blocked table do not poison the anti-match.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL NOT IN entry defines it as the negation of expr IN(value,...), supporting the three-valued-logic diagnosis.

semantic_check.expected: The seed data returns only id 1.
semantic_check.observed: The rewrite tests actual correlated matches and avoids applying NOT to a NULL-bearing IN result.

verification.details: The semantic oracle requires future MySQL execution; only operator documentation was available now.

notes: Runtime test is especially important for this three-valued-logic case.

sql: CREATE INDEX idx_roles ON profiles((CAST(roles->'$[*]' AS JSON ARRAY)));
user_problem: A multi-valued JSON index targets JSON ARRAY directly on MySQL 8.0.17, but that CAST target is not allowed for the array index.
schema_context: profiles(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, roles JSON)
expected_behavior: Create a multi-valued index over unsigned integer role identifiers stored in the JSON array.
root_cause: For a multi-valued index, ARRAY is supported from 8.0.17 but JSON is explicitly excluded as the element CAST type.
reference_fix_sql: CREATE INDEX idx_roles ON profiles((CAST(roles->'$[*]' AS UNSIGNED ARRAY)));
reference_explanation: Keep ARRAY but cast each indexed element to an allowed scalar type, UNSIGNED, rather than the forbidden JSON target.

sql: CREATE TABLE charges (amount DOUBLE(10,2) UNSIGNED);
error_message: DOUBLE(M,D) and UNSIGNED for DOUBLE are deprecated as of MySQL 8.0.17.
user_problem: A new billing table copied an old DOUBLE display declaration and now triggers deprecation warnings on MySQL 8.0.17.
expected_behavior: Store nonnegative monetary amounts with two exact fractional digits without deprecated floating syntax.
root_cause: MySQL deprecated both DOUBLE(M,D) and the UNSIGNED attribute for DOUBLE as of 8.0.17; floating point is also a poor exact-money fit.
reference_fix_sql: CREATE TABLE charges (amount DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (amount >= 0));
reference_explanation: Use fixed-point DECIMAL for money and express nonnegativity with CHECK, the alternative suggested for deprecated floating UNSIGNED.

evidence.support_summary: The MySQL DOUBLE entry gives the 8.0.17 deprecations and recommends a CHECK constraint instead of UNSIGNED.

verification.details: Documentation-only; DECIMAL and CHECK behavior was not executed.

notes: The warning description is documented, not observed locally.
